fiba.a1_h1a_l1: Installation and maintenance of FTTH (fibre to the home) networks.
fiba.a1_h1a_l2: Laying cables, connecting enclosures, splicing fibres.
fiba.a1_h1a_l4: Reading plans, following safety rules, mastering the tools.
fiba.a1_h1b_l3: Quality control of installations and advanced fault diagnosis.
fiba.a1_h1c_l3: Keeping up with technology and standards.
fiba.a1_h1c_l4: Supervising network architectures, for example passive optical networks (PON).
fiba.a1_h2_p: There are several ways into the trade: technical education in electricity or networks, a short practice-focused vocational course, or in-company training. Advice from the training team: field experience counts as much as the diploma, because handling fibre is learned by doing it.
fiba.a1_h3a_l1: The main certification of The Fiber Optic Association (FOA) for fibre optic technicians.
fiba.a1_h3a_l2: Written exam of 100 questions (multiple choice, matching, true or false): at least 70 correct answers to pass.
fiba.a1_h3a_l3: Two routes: a course at a FOA-approved school, or at least two years of field experience through its direct certification programme.
fiba.a1_h3b_l1: Obtained by passing the 200-301 CCNA exam, which covers network fundamentals, network access, IP connectivity and services, security fundamentals, automation and programmability.
fiba.a1_h3b_l2: A certification focused on computer networks rather than fibre, useful for moving towards network engineer roles.
fiba.a1_h3_note: Wisy Safety does not issue these certifications: their requirements are set by each organisation and should be checked on its website.
fiba.a1_h4_l1: Rigour and precision: fibre forgives neither dust nor approximation.
fiba.a1_h4_l2: Analysis and diagnosis: reading a measurement, locating a fault.
fiba.a1_h4_l3: Communication: with customers, suppliers, field teams and management.
fiba.a1_h4_l4: Adaptability: technologies and standards evolve, keeping up is part of the job.
fiba.a1_key: Progression relies on training, field practice and, depending on the target job, a professional certification issued by the organisation that owns it.
fiba.a1_src_note: Sections 1, 2 and 4 are advice from the Wisy Safety training team. Information about the certifications comes from the organisations that issue them:
fiba.a2_lead: Fibre types, ITU recommendations, typical losses and measuring instruments: the technical reference points to master, checked against The Fiber Optic Association (FOA) and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
fiba.a2_figcap: Illustration generated by artificial intelligence: it does not show a real optical fibre splice.
fiba.a2_h1_p: An optical fibre expert works throughout the life of a network: design, deployment, commissioning, diagnosis and repair. Depending on the job, they are an optical network engineer (FTTH, FTTB or FTTO architectures), a connection technician (pulling, splicing, connecting), a quality manager (measuring and validating networks) or a deployment project manager.
fiba.a2_h2_p1: Single-mode fibre has a very thin core, about 9 µm: light follows only one mode in it. It is used in particular for telephony and cable TV, with lasers at 1310 and 1550 nm. Multimode fibre has a larger core, almost always 50 or 62.5 µm; it is used at 850 and 1300 nm for local networks.
fiba.a2_h2_p2: As for standards, ITU-T Recommendation G.652 describes a single-mode fibre with zero dispersion around 1310 nm, also usable around 1550 nm; G.657 describes a single-mode fibre less sensitive to bending, designed in particular for access networks and inside buildings. In multimode, OM3 and OM4 fibres (50/125 µm) are optimised for VCSEL laser sources at 850 nm.
fiba.a2_h3_p: Two fibres are joined by splicing — fusion or mechanical — or with connectors. To estimate a link's loss budget, the FOA uses typical losses of about 0.3 dB per connector and 0.15 dB per single-mode fusion splice; for prepolished connectors with a mechanical splice, the maximum value in the TIA-568 standard is 0.75 dB.
fiba.a2_h4_l1: Inspection microscope (100 to 200 times) and cleaning equipment: to check every connector.
fiba.a2_h4_l2: Source and power meter: end-to-end insertion loss measurement, required by standards to qualify a link.
fiba.a2_h4_l3: Visual fault locator (VFL): a visible red laser to trace a fibre and spot a break.
fiba.a2_h4_l4: Reflectometer (OTDR): to check each event on a long link with splices, or for troubleshooting.
fiba.a2_h4_p: A good habit, recommended by the training team: inspect and clean each connector before connecting or measuring it.
fiba.a2_h5_p: To have your skills recognised, you can aim for a certification issued by a third-party organisation, such as the FOA's CFOT for fibre technicians, or Cisco's CCNA for computer networks. Their requirements are detailed in the article on career paths.
fiba.a2_h6_l1: Rigour in preparation, cleanliness and checking.
fiba.a2_h6_l2: A sense of diagnosis: reading a trace, interpreting a measurement.
fiba.a2_h6_l4: Curiosity: technologies evolve, keeping up is part of the job.
fiba.a2_key: A link is judged by its measurements: the measured loss is compared with the loss budget estimated from the typical losses of the fibre, connectors and splices.
